translations.text: Discourse of Saint Hippolytus on the Faith
1.1 We believe as we were baptized, and we glorify as we were enlightened by the baptism of the font.
We believe in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, as the Savior said to the disciples in the Gospel:
"Go now and make disciples of all the nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"
for the essence of the wondrous Trinity is one. 1.2 We believe in and confess the Father unbegotten, perfect God, and the Son begotten of the Father of light,
perfect God, and the Holy Spirit, giver of graces, perfect God: one Godhead, one nature, one will, three names of the perfect Trinity.
2.1 But how great is the essence of his riches! Who among human beings could be able to express the Godhead truly, as it is?
But in the measure that this weakness of ours is able, he himself willed it and showed us, for "no one knows God
except the Spirit of God and the Son, who came and told us and revealed and showed us." For he says: "Whoever has seen me has seen my Father."
But how are we able to tell of it, we who stand nailed fast in the form of this image of ours, as the Creator created us?
2.2 Now how then shall we proclaim God by means of this image of ours, we who are made of members, fitted together [?] and molded from earth?
Each member has its own particular function and cannot do the function of its neighbor:
the eye does not hear, nor does the ear see, nor does the tongue smell, nor do the hands walk, nor do the feet cry out.
The mouth is for food, the nostrils for smelling, the palate for perceiving taste.
Each is bound to its own nature and stays there. 2.3 But this much only we believe and know, that he is the true God,
and not how he is; who is able to tell of God, who is light in every way; in every way a hearer; in every way a seer;
in every way as much as he himself is; in every way he is power, in every way he is wisdom, living Spirit, consuming fire; immeasurable and unchangeable;
inexpressible glory; power that cannot be looked upon; riches, goodness, likeness, wonder, unreachable by minds and thoughts, beyond all words.
Neither the sight of the eyes nor the hearing of the ears nor the imaginings of the heart can attain to what he is.
The heavens entirely, and the world wholly, and all the ends of the sky cannot hold him up;
and by his word he bears up and holds all things, and he suspends them from the power of his command.
And he himself stands and encompasses all things: beneath all and above all, outside of all; and all things are with him and all things are his, and all glory is his.
3.1 And from time to time he spoke to our holy fathers in inexpressible visions,
in [?] changes of form, not that the Godhead is really like that, but it appears to us only according to this weakness of ours;
and he himself abides in his own Godhead and is eternal, in wondrous fire, in praised goodness and beauty, the image of the Godhead,
3.2 For God is unreachable and immeasurable and indivisible and unsearchable and untouchable, and he cannot be comprehended; he is not manifest to the sight of any created beings.
He is near to all, yet no one has known his name, and there is no other before him who from then until now could give him a name, for everything is from him.
But he himself exists by his own essence; he is invisible to the thought of hearts, and the nature of his being is unsearchable.
With him there is power over all that is impossible. Now who is able to see and search out such might?
Rather, he himself appears only as far as anyone is able to see. 3.3 Now the maker of all, the creator of all,
the ruler of all, the all-knowing, the Lord of all, the holder of all, the one abounding in all things, the healer of all,
the all-wise, in his manifestation to the righteous, himself conceals his terrible majesty, so that he may bring them near to his divinity,
and he appears in the image of men and in the likeness of angels, so that those holy ones may become able to see him with the eyes of their minds.
4.1 Let us truly hold firm this holy faith, in which the holy books, by the eternal Holy Spirit, clearly and face to face instruct us concerning the kingdom of God,
which was revealed in converse to our righteous fathers.
And he spoke through his Son and the Holy Spirit, and it was proclaimed to the world through the holy prophets and apostles, and the firmness of faith was given to us,
so that by faith we may stand in the truth. 4.2 One God, Father and Lord, creator of all, and the only-begotten Son,
who is from the Father and with the Father and toward the Father, and his Holy Spirit, who is from his essence, and in unity he made all things;
which is one lordship, one power, one dominion, one authority, one headship, one wealth, one knowledge, one beginningless might.
One perfect Trinity, one perfect will in the ineffable and unsearchable single unity of the Trinity,
one essence, one nature, one divinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, three names, one power of divinity.

4.3 The Father himself, and the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Father and with the Son, pure in the nature of their essence, consubstantial, equal in depths, heights, breadths and lengths;
which passes through all created things -- those of heaven and earth, breezes and winds, fire and water, light and darkness, the abysses of the depths and the heights,
which with its light instantly reaches and passes through invisible creatures and powers, and its nature cannot be grasped by anyone, the one crown of the Trinity.
And heaven and earth are full of his glory [?], as King Solomon, the son of the prophet, says by the Holy Spirit in his prayer:
"Heaven and earth cannot contain God." And another prophet calls the heavens a throne, and the earth the footstool of his feet.
And now he whom all created things cannot contain has his rest with the quiet and the lowly,
who tremble at his words and who fear his name; with them he establishes his dwelling.
5.1 This is the wealth of the unity of the Holy Trinity in its naming.
And this is not hidden from the wise, namely that the Father is unbegotten and begetter, and the Son is not a begetter but is begotten of the Father,
and the Holy Spirit is neither begetter nor begotten, but proceeding and spreading abroad, in accordance with the word that says:
"The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father." 5.2 And he is not called brother of the Son, for he is not an offspring, nor is he alien to God,
for he proceeds from the Father, just as Eve and Abel are not called brother and sister to each other, although both of them are from Adam:
the one by creation and the other by birth. Nor is Adam called the father of Eve, although that rib was taken from him.

In the same way, although the Son and the Holy Spirit are from God, they are not called brothers to each other, for their orderings in relation to one another are evident from that one fullness of the essence of the Father.
6.1 We confess and know the Father as without beginning, unmanifest, incomprehensible, ineffable, incorruptible, immeasurable, indivisible, simple, pure, without parts, unbegotten,
immeasurable, without beginning, boundless, unmixed, incorporeal, conceived beforehand [?], knowing [?] before all creatures and made things. 6.2 And the Son as begotten, only-begotten,
without beginning, without time, ineffable, without division, indivisible, inseparable, without sufferings, undivided, without intermediaries,
begotten before all times and from that eternal Father, for he is begotten divinely from God and not humanly, by the ordering of times.
Nor did he come forth through an impulse that produces seed, or through any affliction, which is far from the Godhead, but in holiness and purity,
as it befits the Godhead to beget: thus, in likeness to what he himself is, as the disk of the sun begets light, as a spring begets water.
6.3 So it is evident that the one begotten of God is from his very essence, and is like him, and is according to him, and is himself God.

He was begotten and was not separated; he came from the Father and did not depart from him, but he is from the Father, and is forever, and is at all times, and stands complete in his own very essence.
And who is there who could explain this to us clearly, if not the evangelist and theologian John, who said:
"No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten God, who is from the bosom of the Father; he has told us"?
7. And the Holy Spirit is proceeding, everlasting, eternal from the Father, henceforth the Holy Spirit, Spirit of the mouth of God, upright Spirit, Spirit of [?], Spirit of goodness,
Spirit of nobility, Spirit of wisdom and knowledge, Spirit of counsel and might, Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, and is of the same essence as the Father and the Son.
He is not created, nor is he a slave who receives commands, but a giver of commands,
not under command nor under a task, but a fellow worker, for the work of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one;
for the Holy Spirit is God, and he does that same work of the Father and the Son with authority, by his own will, for he is liberator and savior, and he gives the law,
He distributes the gift as he wills and fills all things; for the powers on high also cry out and say:
"Holy, holy, holy!" They say "holy" three times and "Lord" once, for the lordship of the Holy Trinity is one.
8.1 Do you see the true unity and Trinity? And it is not that we speak of separate gods; they are not called three gods, for they are not of one essence and another.
Nor again is it called only one, so that we may not turn aside to Judaism and to the thinking of the Sabellians; rather, we believe in a Trinity of persons, a fullness in unity.
And we do not speak of three gods, so that we may not be like the pagans, who speak of many gods.
8.2 And those who have turned away from this true faith have strayed into error, as the Saviour says in the Gospel:
"I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name, and him you will receive." 6.3 Paul bears witness to the same thing and says:
"Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, he will send upon them the delusion of error,
so that they may believe the deceiver, and that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth."
9.1 But let us hold firmly to that true and good confession, for faith has not been given to all,
but to those to whom it has been granted by the Father of light, and who by their own selves have been helped and offered up [?], as the prophet said by the Holy Spirit:
"They shall all be named by God." And then he says: "I will put my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts.
And they shall be my people, and I will be their God." 9.2 And he, the very one, the eternal one, the one born without beginning from the Father, and the power,
and the divinity, and the Word, God born from the Father, who is before all ages, the same one the offspring of God, the same one the divinity, born from the Father.
He who is before all ages, the same Son of God, came for our salvation and put on this man, and was born of the holy Virgin in the flesh at the end of times, yet not by confusion or by [?];
9.3 Father and Son and holy [?] (the text reads "daughter"; perhaps "Spirit"): at the time of the [?] of that holy Virgin in the flesh, let us call them to mind so as to understand,
but on account of the inseparability and indivisibility of essence, on account of the unity of will and the unity, yes; but as for each individually, no.
For just as we understand the begetting from the Father and recognize the begotten Son, and confess the procession of the Holy Spirit from him, so too the sending of the Son by the Father alone.

And the second birth, from the Virgin, belongs to the Son of God as his own and his alone; and the sanctification of the Virgin's womb, and its sanctification as a temple, belongs to the Holy Spirit alone:
for the Holy Trinity is not one name, but truly three perfect personal names.
10.1 Now, him whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain, how then could the heart of man contain him?
Is man perhaps greater than heaven and earth, or than all created things?
Now understand that whatever God wills comes to be, and whatever he wants, he has also done. And whatever he wishes, he also does, and what he wills does not fail.
But he humbled himself, made himself small, and became as he wished. 10.2 God sent his Son into the world,
who came and was born of a holy woman; the Lord was sent by God and by the Holy Spirit.
The Son himself came and was born of the Virgin himself, of his own self, with authority, as he wished, according to that saying:
"I have power to lay down my life, and I have power again to take it up."
He came and fulfilled the will of the one who sent him, according to the word he spoke, saying:
"I came to fulfill the will of my Father," so that he might show us the unity of the Trinity, itself inseparable and indivisible, by that unity of essence, by the will of the Father.
10.3 And he entered the womb of the Virgin and did not abhor it, for he himself was the sanctifier of all, and of his own will he was wrapped in swaddling clothes;

and the ancient Godhead became a child for our sake, and he who was immeasurable and incomprehensible in the fullness of the Godhead came down for our sake, humbled himself, and was contained in flesh.
He appeared fully and truly in bodily form, according to the word the Apostle spoke, saying:
"Not by measure did he give him the Spirit." 10.4 Although he put on flesh and was born like us, yet the Godhead did not change,
but stands in the glory of the Father, in the nature of his Godhead; as it was, so it is and stands forever.
He is with his Father on high in his own nature, as the Lord himself says:
"I myself am the same and have not changed." 10.5 Although he took on the form of a man, truly became man, and endured insult,
yet that descent, that coming, and that advent are to be understood as his divine manifestation;
and not as if he moved from place to place, he by whom all things are filled and who surrounds all things. 10.6 Although he appeared despised, yet he mingled and united the flesh with his Godhead,
for by the Holy Spirit he sanctified the womb of the Virgin, and the Son of God put on flesh from the holy Virgin,
he by whose hand the foundations of the earth were created and the expanses of the heavens were spread out, 10.7 concerning whom the prophet also says:
"The Lord has revealed his right hand and his arm to all the Gentiles. And all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God."
He himself is the right hand of the Father, Christ is his arm, and through him his creatures were enlightened, and he destroyed the evil one by his flesh.
And he condemned sin through the flesh which the Godhead put on. 10.8 That Height which put on lowliness, the Invisible One in a despised appearance,
for whom at that very time the hosts of heaven raised a hymn of praise to God with a loud cry, and instructed the shepherds, and praised the height and the lowliness of the Son, saying:

"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace," so that the shepherds might not think him contemptible because of the manger and the swaddling clothes. 10.9 For the Psalmist bears witness in his hymn:
"Before the morning star was his name, and in him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed."
By this word he tells us of the birth in the flesh, and by the other he shows us the Godhead, when he said:
"From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you." Only the unbegotten Father, who begot him, knows it.
But this second birth he made manifest among men by his grace, so that he might save men and bring them into blessing out of the first curse, and might renew the earth by his blessing,
by his coming. 10.10 For among all the graces of God there is nothing greater than this:
God the Word became man for the salvation of the world and was born of the holy Virgin.
And in place of the curses and maledictions upon the womb of all women, he would sow the blessing of his own graces,

10.11 for because of Eve all the races of women were cursed, and on account of Mary they received the blessing from on high, for he saw human beings in perdition, gathered the scattered and found the lost.
And that grace-bearing Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, without a man, her holy womb remaining uncorrupted,
the Son of God, in that incomprehensible manner, and in the manner of women who give birth she bore the firstborn in the city of David, Bethlehem.
11.1 There, from that time on, the spiritual narrators, the chronicles of the prophets, are fulfilled concerning the child who was born,
the son given to us, who has dominion upon his own shoulders, and his name was called Angel of Great Counsel,
Wonderful Counselor, mighty God and Sovereign, Prince of Peace and Father of the world that is prepared.
11.2 Do you see that he is Son and Prince and Angel and Counselor and mighty God 11.3 and Father of the world that is prepared?
For this child born today shows us that the Son existed even before, for he is the power of God and Counselor and mighty God, by whom these ages were established.
And he is a child, for today he was born of the holy Virgin in Bethlehem, concerning whom it is foretold to us: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son, and today I have begotten you."
And he is Father of the world that is prepared, for this world is grown old and mortal, like that first man who came from the earth.
This second man, come from heaven, was born of a virgin in order to renew that first man, and he is ruler by this,
for Isaiah speaks of the rod sprung up from the roots of Jesse, and by the flower from that shoot he speaks of the birth from that daughter of David.
If it is so, he will also sit on the throne of David, and his kingdom will prosper.
11.4 The Son, ever glorified by the spiritual beings and by those fire-like watchers, came and became man, so that humankind might be able to see him.
But that first birth of the Godhead from the Father, the Father himself knows;
For no one can search out even this second birth of the Son in the flesh, for the prophet says:
"Who can declare his generation?" For no one has ever seen God in his essence, not even the powers of heaven.
11.5 But the Son, born in the flesh, became perfect man, and through that perfect Godhead revealed to us the power of the Godhead.
Of whom John too says in his writings:
"That which was from the beginning, which we heard and saw with the eye, which we looked upon, and our hands served the word of life;
and that life appeared, and we saw it and testify, for it is true and life eternal."
11.6 He, God the Word, who cannot be seized or assailed, put on that flesh, and by means of that flesh they assailed and seized him.
And everything that they did to that flesh, he took upon himself of his own will.
Unrevealed, he kept himself hidden and endured in that humility; through that flesh he became a servant and a companion to humankind.
And he freed this flesh of men from sins, he who descended into hell, and from there he brought up those confined in hell.
By the flesh he pursued and drove out the devil, bound sin and nailed it to the wood of the cross, 11.8 for to those who believed in his flesh he made known his divinity.
And those who stumbled at his flesh also denied the nature of his divinity.
For he united the flesh to himself by nature and united the flesh to his divinity.
Those who believed in him delight in ineffable good things, and those who went astray from this faith,
did not walk in straight places, but strayed into the pathless waste and prepared for themselves unsearchable places.
11.9 And many turned aside from the true faith and supposed that they had found something, and they found nothing.
As it is written: "They pursued nothing and found nothing."
12.1 Now all who turn away from this true faith and sow barren and withered,
unploughed, vain and venom-steeped seed in the hearing of those who listen, such people are anathema, even if one be an angel from heaven.
And let him be cursed, like the earth-eating serpent, who by lying and deceitful speech wished to overturn the commandment of the Creator.
And those who are in communion with him and say:
"Once the Son was not, and before he was begotten he did not exist, and he came into being out of nothing, and from some other power, or by emanation and change,"
12.2 such people the catholic Church anathematizes, and also the heresy of Sabellius, which says: "He is one and the same."
But we know the Father as Father, and the Son as Son, and the Spirit as Holy Spirit, one lordship, one divinity, three perfect persons.
Ever Father, ever Son, ever Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, perfect Advocate.
Uncreated, who existed from before and spoke in the Law and in the prophets and apostles,
and came down upon the Jordan and bore witness to the incarnation of the Son of God, as the voice came: "This is my beloved Son,"
13.1 who also put on this perfect man from Mary the God-bearer by the Holy Spirit, flesh and soul, truly and not in figure,
for thus he came to redeem this man wholly; 13.2 for our salvation he became man and lived in the form of men.
He ate and drank as we do, and truly suffered and was beaten and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, was nailed to the cross, died, was buried, and was brought to life.
He rose on the third day, was exalted to heaven, went up, sat at the right hand of God his Father, went up [?], and he will come again to judge the living and the dead. 13.3 And for whom did he die?
Was he perhaps in some way liable to death? Hear what the prophet says:
"He committed no lawlessness, nor was deceit found in his mouth," of whom he himself also says:
"Which of you convicts me of sin?" Or is he in any way liable to death under the Law?
And he himself says: "I came to fulfil the Law." And the blessed apostle bears witness to him, saying:
"Christ is the end of the Law." 13.4 Now a man dies at the hands of tyrants against his own will. But understand this, of which he says:
"I myself lay down my life, and no one shall take it from me." He says: "I myself lay down my life, and afterward I take it up again."
Why does the innocent one, who is not liable to death, wish to lay down his own life? He himself said:
"I am the good shepherd, who lay down my soul for my sheep." For which flock?
For those frightened ones, those fleeing ones, those torn by wild beasts, about whom the prophet spoke beforehand, saying:
"All of us, like sheep, have gone astray, and the Lord gave him up for our sins, and for the iniquities of the people death was lifted up";
by which he also redeemed those carried off as captives from captivity. 13.5 If this is so, then that praiser, the Psalmist, was praising Christ when he said:
"I became like a man without help, free among the dead." For he alone was not enslaved to sin, and not by any other power,
but by his own might he slew mighty death, the devourer of the world, and stilled every tear from all eyes,
so that he might bring the mortality of humankind to life in that immortal kingdom.
14.1 And again, as the prophet says: "He ascended on high and took captivity captive, he took the spoil, divided it as gifts, and gave it to the sons of men."

For by that very thing by which people were taken captive, that worthless idolatry, by that same wood of custom he turned people to the worship of God, and he left us a sign: the cross of his sufferings,
so that the wood of the cross might be for us in place of those carved pieces of wood, and Christ himself, silent [?] on the cross, in place of those defiled man-shaped idols,
who had gone astray toward those [?], and the blood of our Lord in place of the gifts and rejoicings of defilement and the sacrifices,
which they would send before those [?], and they would rejoice. 14.2 The Father has shown it to us in a trustworthy way:
that fatted one was slain, the Son of God, and he called the church to that [?] of the wedding, and there was fulfilled the saying, "He whose bride it is, he is the bridegroom."
For Christ is the bridegroom, and the church the bride. And who are the friends of that bridegroom?
They are those who ate the flesh of that bridegroom and forgot the lawless sacrifice in the assembly before those demons, and that house of iniquity,
the dwelling place of those man-faced idols, and who worshipped in truth the true wood of the cross and that unmixed flesh,

which wiped away the sins of humankind, and together with them the torment and the punishment as well. 14.3 If this is so, then upon those whom he redeemed from that punishment and justified he has bestowed a great gift.
Truly a great gift and honor has been given to us, for through this baptismal font we are called children of God.
And he promised to give us that eternal and boundless gift, that unending and inexpressible and beginningless kingdom of his.
14.4 And as trees, by sprouting and by [?] and flower and seed and leaf and fruit and scent and taste, each one individually, of its own
nature's nakedness is clothed, and becomes recognizable by its scent and taste, and as it was before, so it appears in form, and it does not change into another form.
In the same way a person is clothed and adorned with flesh, sinews, bones, joints, joining-together, skin and hair, and only then does his spirit return to him.
And in whatever state they were buried in the graves, in that same state they will come, bearing their burdens.
15.1 For when he was going up the Mount of Olives, he made a path among the clouds upon the air, he was ascending to the heaven of the Father; he raised his hands,
blessed the disciples and sent them out, so that they might make disciples of all the nations and teach them. 15.2 Concerning all this they proclaimed the true God to the world, and,
as his disciples taught the world, he called them teachers through the Holy Spirit, to whom he also said:
"I have many other things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will remind you and will guide all of you in truth."
And again: "I will go and send the Advocate to you." 15.3 And as the apostle Paul says by the Holy Spirit:
"Truly great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, revealed to angels,
preached among the nations, believed in the world and exalted in glory." 15.4 He ascended and sat at the right hand of God the Father;
and after the day of the Passion, which is the fulfilment, and at the completion of the fifty days, while the apostles were gathered together,
the Holy Spirit came and filled them all, and they began to speak in many languages, as the Spirit gave them to speak in foreign tongues,

because of which Peter too was filled with the Holy Spirit, and with many parables he showed them the coming of the Holy Spirit and the graces of Christ. 15.5 And when they had received the Holy Spirit,
they remembered the word of the Lord, which he had spoken: "John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit."
And then he says: "We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is from God." 15.6 For Christ himself says:
"God is spirit." With these words he shows us the single essence of the Trinity:
"For he will not speak anything on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will tell you what is to come."
He will glorify me, for he will receive from me and tell you, for everything that belongs to my Father is mine.
For this reason I said to you that he will receive from me and tell you."
16.1 Now behold the unity, the oneness of will, the equality of the true Trinity.
And see how the Trinity, in its unity, truly shone forth and was revealed to us. For he says:
"The Holy Spirit will not say anything on his own, but will take from me and tell you, for what my Father has,
is mine." 16.2 Behold the Father perfect, the Son perfect and the Holy Spirit perfect; the Father Creator, the Son Creator, the Holy Spirit Creator.
Of the Father it says: "My Father is working until now." 16.3 And again: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth."
And concerning the Son, the evangelist says: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." And then:
"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established." And concerning the Holy Spirit he says: "and by the spirit of his mouth all their power."
And then Christ says: "It is the Spirit that gives life, and the flesh profits nothing."
He also taught us about the indivisible nature of the Godhead, its undivided power, concerning which he also said:
"I came forth from the Father and came into the world." In the same way he also says of the Holy Spirit: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father."
And by this too he shows us the undivided unity of the Trinity, for he says:
"God is spirit," and he shows us, both concerning himself and concerning the true Spirit,
how he is inseparable from the Father. 16.4 Even though the apostles are said to be sent by the Father, yet it is by the Trinity;
by one will, or by one counsel, or likewise the undivided Trinity accomplished that work in unity, 16.5 concerning which John the Baptist also testifies:
"No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is from the bosom of the Father; he has told us."
For since they saw him as being together with them, the Son and the Holy Spirit were also doers of that work.

Just as the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal in Godhead, so too they had knowledge of the works of the Father. 16.6 O wondrous gift of the knowledge of God, allotted to those apostles!
How they were at once brought forward [?] to such beautiful and fragrant knowledge! In the same manner it is proper to understand concerning that true Holy Spirit what he said:
"The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father." He proceeds and is not divided; he is imparted and is not diminished.
And at the same time he truly speaks of that unity and equality: "I am with the Father and the Father is with me.
And whoever has seen me has seen my Father," for the Godhead is not contained by any boundary.
And now, shall we then say this: that the Father is in heaven, and the only-begotten Son and the true Spirit are on earth, by whom all things are filled, and who is in all and above all?
16.7 About all this he speaks in a divine manner, and instructs and teaches those disciples of Christ.
And they, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached to all the great graces of the teaching of that Son of God, and taught many the true faith.
And by that deed of courage they brought many into submission to that liberating yoke, for on that small occasion they offered up their faith from here to heaven, together with holy deeds.
17.1 Now henceforth the Son of God is mediator and guarantor of unattainable good things for those who love him.
And what indeed could be more unattainable and immeasurable than this: when he who went up to the Father in heaven comes from heaven in the glory of the Father, and before all
those ranks of angels and those mighty hosts takes his beloved ones by the hand, draws them to himself, and gladdens them in that very dwelling of his Godhead?
17.2 For that unfailing and mighty God prepares a dwelling in that place of inheritance, that allotted [?] territory, that endless kingdom,
so that in that one place of delight alone those well-ordered and worthy ones [?].
For the rational and spiritual and bodily ones he will prepare a dwelling with himself, 17.3 concerning which the Savior of all brought good news to those disciples and promised:
"Where I am, there you also will be, and at all times you will behold my glory." But this one thing he simply declares, and he says still more [?]:
"Then you will know that I am with the Father, and you are with me, and I am among you." In this connection that saying should be remembered:
"What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him."
As the blessed Paul says: "Thanks be to Christ for his inexpressible gifts."
17.4 For it was not in vain or carelessly that God the Word humbled himself so far, the only-begotten Son of the God without beginning, truly the true Son of God,
for he humbled himself in order to exalt us; for this reason he took upon himself being called son of David, so that he might make us sons of God.
The Father of the Son accepts that servant, so that the Lord may become a father to you. 17.5 If you doubt anything on the basis of what is yours, believe and learn on the basis of what is his,
for this seems far harder to the human mind: that God became man for this purpose, that man might be called son of God.
18.1 Now, when you hear that the Son of God is son of David and son of Abraham, doubt no longer from now on, as though you, a son of Adam, could not be a son of God.

He was born in the flesh of the holy Virgin so that you might be born of the Holy Spirit. 18.2 He was born of a woman so that you might be born of the baptismal font, by which you have become a son of God.
For this reason he was born a second time and became like us and became higher than us; for birth from a woman is laid upon us, and after this, not from flesh,
nor from blood, but from the Holy Spirit we are born in the holy font. This belongs to him who was born in a way surpassing ours.
And because it was prepared to be fulfilled in us, he made it known to us beforehand. 18.3 For just as he himself was born by that second birth without blood and without the will of the flesh,
so too may we, without blood and without flesh, be born of the Holy Spirit by that birth from above.
18.4 And just as the King, the nature of the Godhead, appeared to us in the form of a man, so too us men, in his own Godhead
and kingship, may he make crowned, and in his kingdom may he gladden us with his unfading heavenly joy.
Glory to his Godhead, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
19.1 From now on, then, let us hold firmly to the good confession which we have confessed. Let us not turn aside, either to the right or to the left!
Let us believe in the Father, perfect God, and the Son, perfect God, and the Holy Spirit, perfect God!
19.2 One is the Godhead of the Holy Trinity, one essence, one nature, one perfect Trinity itself, one perfect God, one power, one might,
one dominion, one united glory, one united in light, one united in fullness, for no one is able to search out what or how he was.
We believe in the Trinity. Believe in the unity without error, in silence. But only believe 19.3 now in the one who is unsearchable and inexpressible.
O, how can those who have come from the earth, who were formed and created, search out or know the Most High, and these creatures who have a beginning, the one who has no beginning?
How can they search out the incomprehensible one? To him belongs glory forever and ever, amen.
